conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospitalists. You're here today for your 15th cycle of high-dose methotrexate for your brain lymphoma. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I'm okay, just a little tired. My breathing’s been off this week—I’ve been using my albuterol more often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I saw that in your chart. We’re thinking it might be acute bronchitis, possibly overlapping with your asthma. We’ll manage it with your usual inhalers and add a new one if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I haven’t had a fever or cough, just shortness of breath when I walk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits. We’ll monitor it. Now, about the chemotherapy—we’ll give you the methotrexate infusion today. We’ll also start IV fluids with sodium acetate to help protect your kidneys and make sure the drug clears properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember from last time. No bicarbonate IV, right? Because of the shortage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re using sodium acetate instead, and you’ll also take oral bicarbonate pills to keep your urine alkaline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And leucovorin starts tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 24 hours after the chemo starts. We’ll also check your methotrexate levels every day to make sure it’s clearing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been nauseated before, but the anti-nausea meds help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you pre-meds for nausea, and you can have more if needed. We’ll also watch your labs closely—especially liver enzymes, which sometimes go up with each cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, the transaminitis. It always comes back a little, but it settles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it’s been mild so far. We’ll keep an eye on it. One thing—we’ve held your aspirin during this admission to help the methotrexate clear faster.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. Because of the blood clot history. When do I restart it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart it when you go home. You should take it daily again, but stop it two days before your next chemo admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll mark that on my calendar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, your mesalamine for ulcerative colitis is on hold while you’re here to avoid interactions. If your symptoms flare up at home, you can restart it—just not during chemo stays.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: After the clindamycin last time, I had bleeding. I was scared. But it’s been quiet since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that was likely antibiotic-related colitis. We’ll avoid unnecessary antibiotics this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. My foot pain is still there—burning, up the leg. Not worse, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on gabapentin for that. Tests were negative before, so we’ll continue managing the symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just wish we knew what was causing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll keep looking if anything changes. For now, we focus on what we can manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your first methotrexate level came back—it’s where we expect it. No signs of toxicity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I did feel a little nauseated yesterday, but the prochlorperazine helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added ondansetron to your discharge meds in case you need stronger anti-nausea coverage at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, thank you. How’s my breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on albuterol-ipratropium, the Combivent inhaler. It helps open airways more than albuterol alone. You should feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve used it twice today. Easier to catch my breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll send that home with you. Also, your potassium and phosphorus were low yesterday, so we’ve been replacing them through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, that explains the muscle cramps. Feels better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, those electrolyte imbalances can happen with the fluids and chemo. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’re doing well. Your latest methotrexate level is down to 0.18, which means it’s clearing nicely. We’ll check one more tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Any word on the MRI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The report just came in. The good news is your lymphoma looks stable—no new lesions or abnormal enhancement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, thank goodness. What about the sinus thing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s still some sinus inflammation—mucosal thickening in a few sinuses. But it’s not worse, and since you don’t have symptoms, we won’t treat it now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Last time I got clindamycin, it messed up my gut. I’d rather avoid antibiotics if I can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Agreed. We’ll hold off unless you develop symptoms like congestion or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my mood? I’ve been sad, but not depressed. I don’t want another psych admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I spoke with Social Work. You’re continuing citalopram, which is important. We won’t push a psych consult unless you change your mind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just need support, not another hospital stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your final methotrexate level is 0.13—excellent clearance. Your labs are stable, and you’re breathing better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discharging you. Restart your aspirin tomorrow. Stop it two days before your next chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the new inhaler?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the Combivent as needed for shortness of breath. It’s for possible bronchitis. Keep using your regular asthma inhalers too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the MRI results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call Dr. ___’s office in a few days to get the detailed results. But the key point is your lymphoma is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you for your next cycle.
